description.value: An exploratory voxel-based morphometric analysis examined whether pre-quit regional gray matter volume was associated with a 4-week smoking cessation treatment outcome in adult dependent smokers.

spans.text: In the present exploratory analysis, we sought to identify brain structural predictors of a smoking cessation treatment outcome—point prevalence abstinence at 4 weeks.

In this preliminary analysis, we found associations between regional GM volume, as measured by VBM with DARTEL, and a smoking cessation outcome.
Of 18 participants, 8 successfully met the criteria to be considered quitters.
Among those participants classified as relapsers ( n = 10), 9 provided self-reports of smoking since their previous visit; 1 participant was lost to contact and was presumed to have relapsed.

After controlling for all covariates, compared to relapsers, quitters exhibited significantly higher GM volume in left putamen and right occipital lobe, while also significantly lower GM volume in bilateral hippocampus and right cuneus.

After controlling for all covariates, compared to relapsers, quitters exhibited significantly higher GM volume in left putamen and right occipital lobe, while also significantly lower GM volume in bilateral hippocampus and right cuneus.

Participants had to be interested in quitting smoking, smoke ≥15 cigarettes per day (of a brand of cigarette having an FTC nicotine yield of 0.5 mg) for ≥2 years, have an afternoon breath carbon monoxide (CO) level >15 ppm, with no current smokeless tobacco use, be right-handed, be free of serious health problems and medications altering central nervous system functioning, test negative for illicit drug use, not have any conditions making magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) unsafe, and, among female participants, not pregnant or nursing.

In order to examine differences in GM volume between participants who were able to achieve a 4-week point prevalence abstinence (quitters) versus relapsers, a two-sample t test was conducted in SPM with years smoked and cigarettes per day as covariates.
